items.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009
items.q: Max Roach and Art Blakey and Elvin Jones, you know that changed my way of playing

ctx.x: So most of your people that you listened to, you saw them in New York, you’re — it’s sort of people that you wanted to emulate or heard on records? Is that right?

Yeah. I mean like a lot of the players that I listened to like Philly Joe Jones was my first love and Max Roach and Art Blakey and Elvin Jones, you know that changed my way of playing because I heard in Philly Joe Jones the way he stretched out phrases. You know, and he would just do it for a little while, like he would stretch the phrase out and just for maybe two or three bars, then he would go back to the swing. And I was wondering, I’d say wow, I wonder what would happen if he just kept stretching it out?…
Henry did you ever get, in those days, playing with someone where you felt wow, I’m in way over my head here. I don’t know what to do with this musician?

items.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I didn’t get along with Rashied that well. First thing, I don’t know what he was thinking about, but we were playing at The Village Gate

ctx.x: When did you leave John Coltrane?

1966. I didn’t get along with Rashied that well. First thing, I don’t know what he was thinking about, but we were playing at The Village Gate and I always went early to get set up so I knew everything. When I went out and came back, when it’s almost time to start, he’s moved my drums and put his all over. I said, “What are you doing here?” We had that going. I said, “Well if we are going to play together we have to be coordinated. Otherwise it’s going to sound like it’s just a mess.”
